Fourier Transforms and the DFT

Purdue University
Course-material provenance

This page was migrated from the CHM 696 course materials developed by Jonathan Hood and Lyudmila Slipchenko. Equations and examples remain under editorial review during the Fall 2026 website migration.

Learning goals¶

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

  • apply a consistent forward/inverse Fourier-transform convention;

  • use shift, derivative, convolution, and Parseval identities;

  • explain sampling and frequency bins in the discrete Fourier transform; and

  • derive the radix-2 FFT recurrence and its O(nlog⁡n)O(n\log n)O(nlogn) cost.

Fourier series¶

The complex form of the Fourier series is given by:

f(x)=∑k=−∞∞Ckeikωxf(x) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k e^{i k\omega x}f(x)=k=−∞∑∞​Ck​eikωx
(1)

The complex coefficients CnC_nCn​ are determined by:

Ck=12L∫−LLf(x)e−ikωx dxC_k = \frac{1}{2L} \int_{-L}^L f(x) e^{-ik\omega x} \, dxCk​=2L1​∫−LL​f(x)e−ikωxdx
(2)

The complex exponentials are orthogonal:

12L∫−LLeimωxe−inωx dx=δmn.\frac{1}{2L} \int_{-L}^L e^{im\omega x} e^{-in\omega x} \, dx = \delta_{mn}.2L1​∫−LL​eimωxe−inωxdx=δmn​.
(3)

Fourier series (continued)¶

We can think of a Fourier series as just a change of coordinates of a function f(x)f(x)f(x) into an infinite-dimensional orthogonal function space spanned by sines and cosines ψk=eikx=cos⁡(kx)+isin⁡(kx)\psi_k = e^{i kx} = \cos(kx) + i \sin(kx)ψk​=eikx=cos(kx)+isin(kx). Indeed, for a function f(x)f(x)f(x) defined on interval (−π,π)(-\pi, \pi)(−π,π):

f(x)=∑k=−∞∞ckψk(x)=12π∑k=−∞∞⟨ψk(x),f(x)⟩ψk(x),f(x) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} c_k \psi_k(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \langle \psi_k(x), f(x)\rangle \psi_k(x),f(x)=k=−∞∑∞​ck​ψk​(x)=2π1​k=−∞∑∞​⟨ψk​(x),f(x)⟩ψk​(x),
(4)

with coefficients given by ck=12π⟨ψk(x),f(x)⟩c_k = \frac{1}{2\pi}\langle \psi_k(x), f(x)\rangleck​=2π1​⟨ψk​(x),f(x)⟩

Comparison of Fourier Series and Fourier Transform¶

Fourier Series Fourier Transform

f(x)=∑n=−∞∞cneinω0xf(x) = \sum\limits_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} c_n e^{in\omega_0 x}f(x)=n=−∞∑∞​cn​einω0​x f(x)=F−1(f^(ω))=12π∫−∞∞f^(ω)eiωxdωf(x) = \mathcal{F}^{-1}(\hat{f}(\omega)) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int\limits_{-\infty}^{\infty} \hat{f}(\omega) e^{i\omega x} d\omegaf(x)=F−1(f^​(ω))=2π1​−∞∫∞​f^​(ω)eiωxdω cn=1T∫−T/2T/2f(x)e−inω0xdxc_n = \frac{1}{T} \int\limits_{-T/2}^{T/2} f(x) e^{-in\omega_0 x} dxcn​=T1​−T/2∫T/2​f(x)e−inω0​xdx f^(ω)=F(f(x))=∫−∞∞f(x)e−iωxdx\hat{f}(\omega) = \mathcal{F}(f(x)) = \int\limits_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) e^{-i\omega x} dxf^​(ω)=F(f(x))=−∞∫∞​f(x)e−iωxdx

Fourier transform of a Gaussian function¶

A normalized Gaussian distribution f(t)f(t)f(t), centered on t=0t=0t=0:

f(t)=1τ2πexp⁡(−t22τ2),−∞<t<∞f(t) = \frac{1}{\tau \sqrt{2\pi}} \exp \left( - \frac{t^2}{2\tau^2} \right), \quad -\infty < t < \inftyf(t)=τ2π​1​exp(−2τ2t2​),−∞<t<∞
(5)

A root mean square deviation (or "spread") in time is Δt=τ\Delta t = \tauΔt=τ.

The Fourier transform f^(ω)\hat{f}(\omega)f^​(ω) of f(t)f(t)f(t):

f^(ω)=exp⁡(−τ2ω22)\hat{f}(\omega) = \exp \left( - \frac{\tau^2 \omega^2}{2} \right)f^​(ω)=exp(−2τ2ω2​)
(6)

The Gaussian amplitude has reciprocal width parameters: τ\tauτ in time and 1/τ1/\tau1/τ in angular frequency. If widths are instead defined as the standard deviations of the normalized intensities ∣f(t)∣2|f(t)|^2∣f(t)∣2 and ∣f^(ω)∣2|\hat f(\omega)|^2∣f^​(ω)∣2, then

Δt=τ2,Δω=12τ,Δt Δω=12.\Delta t=\frac{\tau}{\sqrt{2}}, \qquad \Delta\omega=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\tau}, \qquad \Delta t\,\Delta\omega=\frac{1}{2}.Δt=2​τ​,Δω=2​τ1​,ΔtΔω=21​.
(7)

Thus a narrower signal in time necessarily has a broader frequency spectrum.

Time-Shifting Property¶

The time-shifting property states that a shift in the time domain corresponds to a phase shift in the frequency domain:

If F{f(t)}=F(ω)\mathcal{F}\{f(t)\} = F(\omega)F{f(t)}=F(ω), then

F{f(t−t0)}=e−iωt0F(ω)\mathcal{F}\{f(t-t_0)\} = e^{-i\omega t_0}F(\omega)F{f(t−t0​)}=e−iωt0​F(ω)
(8)

This property is crucial in understanding how delays in signals affect their frequency content.

Proof:

F{f(t−t0)}=∫−∞∞f(t−t0)e−iωtdt=∫−∞∞f(u)e−iω(u+t0)du(let u=t−t0)=e−iωt0∫−∞∞f(u)e−iωudu=e−iωt0F(ω)\begin{aligned} \mathcal{F}\{f(t-t_0)\} &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t-t_0)e^{-i\omega t}dt \\ &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(u)e^{-i\omega (u+t_0)}du \quad \text{(let $u = t-t_0$)} \\ &= e^{-i\omega t_0}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(u)e^{-i\omega u}du \\ &= e^{-i\omega t_0}F(\omega) \end{aligned}F{f(t−t0​)}​=∫−∞∞​f(t−t0​)e−iωtdt=∫−∞∞​f(u)e−iω(u+t0​)du(let u=t−t0​)=e−iωt0​∫−∞∞​f(u)e−iωudu=e−iωt0​F(ω)​
(9)

Fourier transform: summary¶

F(eiω0t)=2πδ(ω−ω0)\mathcal{F}( e^{i\omega_0t} ) = 2\pi \delta(\omega-\omega_0)F(eiω0​t)=2πδ(ω−ω0​)
(10)
F(cos⁡(ω0t))=π[δ(ω−ω0)+δ(ω+ω0)]\mathcal{F}(\cos(\omega_0t)) = \pi [\delta(\omega-\omega_0) + \delta(\omega+\omega_0)]F(cos(ω0​t))=π[δ(ω−ω0​)+δ(ω+ω0​)]
(11)
F(dfdt)=iωF(f(t))\mathcal{F}(\frac{df}{dt}) = i\omega \mathcal{F}(f(t))F(dtdf​)=iωF(f(t))
(12)
F(f(t−t0))=e−iωt0F(ω)\mathcal{F}(f(t-t_0)) = e^{-i\omega t_0}F(\omega)F(f(t−t0​))=e−iωt0​F(ω)
(13)

Convolution¶

The continuous convolution of f(t)f(t)f(t) and g(t)g(t)g(t) is defined as:

(f∗g)(t)=∫−∞∞f(τ)g(t−τ) dτ(f * g)(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(\tau) g(t - \tau) \, d\tau(f∗g)(t)=∫−∞∞​f(τ)g(t−τ)dτ
(14)

The convolution is commutative,

(f∗g)(t)=(g∗f)(t)(f * g)(t) = (g * f)(t)(f∗g)(t)=(g∗f)(t)
(15)

The proof for commutativity comes from a quick change of variables by setting u=t−τu = t - \tauu=t−τ, which implies du=−dτdu = -d\taudu=−dτ. Substituting into the integral:

(f∗g)(t)=∫∞−∞f(t−u)g(u)(−du)(f * g)(t) = \int_{\infty}^{-\infty} f(t - u) g(u) (-du)(f∗g)(t)=∫∞−∞​f(t−u)g(u)(−du)
(16)

Flipping the limits of integration to absorb the negative sign:

(f∗g)(t)=∫−∞∞f(t−u)g(u) du(f * g)(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t - u) g(u) \, du(f∗g)(t)=∫−∞∞​f(t−u)g(u)du
(17)

This is exactly the form of (g∗f)(t)(g * f)(t)(g∗f)(t)

Convolution and cross-correlation¶

One common cross-correlation convention is

(f⋆g)(t)=∫−∞∞f∗(τ) g(τ+t) dτ.(f\star g)(t) =\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f^*(\tau)\,g(\tau+t)\,d\tau.(f⋆g)(t)=∫−∞∞​f∗(τ)g(τ+t)dτ.
(18)

Unlike convolution, correlation conjugates one input and does not use the same reflection-and-shift operation. For real functions it measures their overlap as a function of relative shift.

What the original figure plots. It shows graphical comparison of convolution and cross-correlation.

What this is trying to convey. Convolution includes a reflection before shifting and integrating; cross-correlation compares relative shifts.

Polished version.

Convolution Theorem¶

The Convolution Theorem is a fundamental principle in signal processing and Fourier analysis. It states that under suitable conditions, the Fourier transform of the convolution of two functions is equal to the product of their Fourier transforms.

F{f(t)∗g(t)}=F(ω)G(ω)\mathcal{F}\{ f(t) * g(t) \} = F(\omega) G(\omega)F{f(t)∗g(t)}=F(ω)G(ω)
(19)
F−1{F(ω)G(ω)}=f(t)∗g(t)=∫−∞∞f(τ)g(t−τ) dτ\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{ F(\omega) G(\omega) \} = f(t) * g(t) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(\tau) g(t - \tau) \, d\tauF−1{F(ω)G(ω)}=f(t)∗g(t)=∫−∞∞​f(τ)g(t−τ)dτ
(20)

This theorem provides a powerful link between operations in the time domain and the frequency domain:

  • Convolution in the time domain corresponds to multiplication in the frequency domain.

  • Multiplication in the time domain corresponds to convolution in the frequency domain.

With the transform normalization used here, the second identity includes a factor:

F{f(t)g(t)}(ω)=12π(F∗G)(ω).\mathcal{F}\{f(t)g(t)\}(\omega) =\frac{1}{2\pi}(F*G)(\omega).F{f(t)g(t)}(ω)=2π1​(F∗G)(ω).
(21)

Proof of the Convolution Theorem¶

Suppose F{f(t)}=F(ω)\mathcal{F}\{ f(t) \} = F(\omega)F{f(t)}=F(ω) and F{g(t)}=G(ω)\mathcal{F}\{ g(t) \} = G(\omega)F{g(t)}=G(ω). Then, the Fourier transform of the convolution of f(t)f(t)f(t) and g(t)g(t)g(t) is:

F{(f∗g)(t)}=∫−∞∞(f∗g)(t) e−iωt dt=∫−∞∞(∫−∞∞f(τ)g(t−τ) dτ)e−iωt dt=∫−∞∞f(τ)(∫−∞∞g(t−τ)e−iωt dt)dτ=∫−∞∞f(τ)e−iωτ(∫−∞∞g(u)e−iωu du)dτ=F(ω)G(ω)\begin{aligned} \mathcal{F}\{ (f * g)(t) \} &= \int_{-\infty}^\infty (f * g)(t) \, e^{- i \omega t} \, dt \\ &= \int_{-\infty}^\infty \left( \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(\tau) g(t - \tau) \, d\tau \right) e^{- i \omega t} \, dt \\ &= \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(\tau) \left( \int_{-\infty}^\infty g(t - \tau) e^{- i \omega t} \, dt \right) d\tau \\ &= \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(\tau) e^{- i \omega \tau} \left( \int_{-\infty}^\infty g(u) e^{- i \omega u} \, du \right) d\tau \\ &= F(\omega) G(\omega) \end{aligned}F{(f∗g)(t)}​=∫−∞∞​(f∗g)(t)e−iωtdt=∫−∞∞​(∫−∞∞​f(τ)g(t−τ)dτ)e−iωtdt=∫−∞∞​f(τ)(∫−∞∞​g(t−τ)e−iωtdt)dτ=∫−∞∞​f(τ)e−iωτ(∫−∞∞​g(u)e−iωudu)dτ=F(ω)G(ω)​
(22)

In the second-to-last line, we used the change of variables u=t−τu = t - \tauu=t−τ.

Example: Solving heat equation using Fourier transform¶

  • The Heat (Diffusion) Equation in the Spatial Domain:

∂u∂t=α2∂2u∂x2orut=α2uxx\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \alpha^2 \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} \quad \text{or} \quad u_t = \alpha^2 u_{xx}∂t∂u​=α2∂x2∂2u​orut​=α2uxx​
(23)

where u(t,x)u(t,x)u(t,x) is the temperature distribution in time and space,
α\alphaα is the thermal diffusivity constant.

  • Apply the Fourier transform in space:

F(u(t,x))=u^(t,ω)\mathcal{F}(u(t, x)) = \hat{u}(t,\omega)F(u(t,x))=u^(t,ω)
(24)

.

  • Utilize the property of the Fourier transform derivatives :

F(uxx)=(iω)2u^=−ω2u^\mathcal{F}(u_{xx}) = (\text{i}\omega)^2 \hat{u} = -\omega^2 \hat{u}F(uxx​)=(iω)2u^=−ω2u^
(25)

  • Applying this transformation, the original PDE is converted into an ODE for each fixed frequency ω\omegaω:

u^t=−α2ω2u^\hat{u}_t = -\alpha^2 \omega^2 \hat{u}u^t​=−α2ω2u^
(26)

Example: Solving heat equation using Fourier transform (continued)¶

  • The resulting ODE in the frequency domain has a straightforward exponential solution

u^(t,ω)=e−α2ω2tu^(0,ω)\hat{u}(t, \omega) = e^{-\alpha^2\omega^2 t} \hat{u}(0, \omega)u^(t,ω)=e−α2ω2tu^(0,ω)
(27)

where u^(0,ω)\hat{u}(0, \omega)u^(0,ω) is the Fourier transform of the initial temperature distribution u(0,x)u(0, x)u(0,x).

This solution shows that higher frequencies (larger ω\omegaω) decay more rapidly.

  • To find the solution u(t,x)u(t, x)u(t,x) in the original coordinates, the inverse Fourier transform is applied to u^(t,ω)\hat{u}(t, \omega)u^(t,ω):

u(t,x)=F−1(u^(t,ω))u(t, x) = \mathcal{F}^{-1}(\hat{u}(t, \omega))u(t,x)=F−1(u^(t,ω))
(28)

Using the convolution theorem, the solution is the convolution of the initial condition u(0,x)u(0, x)u(0,x) with the inverse transform of the Gaussian term, which is also a Gaussian:

u(t,x)=F−1(e−α2ω2t)∗u(0,x)=12απte−x24α2t∗u(0,x)u(t, x) = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\left(e^{-\alpha^2\omega^2 t}\right) \ast u(0, x) = \frac{1}{2\alpha \sqrt{\pi t}} e^{-\frac{x^2}{4 \alpha^2 t}} \ast u(0, x)u(t,x)=F−1(e−α2ω2t)∗u(0,x)=2απt​1​e−4α2tx2​∗u(0,x)
(29)

Parseval’s Theorem¶

For complex waves, the power or intensity is related to the square of the wave’s amplitude: I=∣x(t)∣2I = |x(t)|^2I=∣x(t)∣2.
The total energy in a signal over all time is given by:

E=∫−∞∞∣x(t)∣2 dtE = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x(t)|^2 \, dtE=∫−∞∞​∣x(t)∣2dt
(30)

We can also analyze signals in the frequency domain using the Fourier transform: X(ω)=F{x(t)}X(\omega) = \mathcal{F}\{ x(t) \}X(ω)=F{x(t)}

Parseval’s theorem relates the energy of a signal in the time domain to its energy in the frequency domain:

∫−∞∞∣x(t)∣2 dt=12π∫−∞∞∣X(ω)∣2 dω\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x(t)|^2 \, dt = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |X(\omega)|^2 \, d\omega∫−∞∞​∣x(t)∣2dt=2π1​∫−∞∞​∣X(ω)∣2dω
(31)

[The total energy of a signal is preserved whether we consider it in the time domain or the frequency domain.]{style=“color: blue”}

Parseval’s Theorem (continued)¶

Parseval’s Theorem:

∫−∞∞∣x(t)∣2 dt=12π∫−∞∞∣X(ω)∣2 dω\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x(t)|^2 \, dt = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |X(\omega)|^2 \, d\omega∫−∞∞​∣x(t)∣2dt=2π1​∫−∞∞​∣X(ω)∣2dω
(32)

This theorem states that the total energy can also be obtained by integrating ∣X(ω)∣2|X(\omega)|^2∣X(ω)∣2 over the frequency domain.
With this Fourier convention, ∣X(ω)∣2/(2π)|X(\omega)|^2/(2\pi)∣X(ω)∣2/(2π) is the spectral energy density with respect to angular frequency.

Proof of Parseval’s Theorem¶

Start with the inverse Fourier transform:

f(t)=12π∫−∞∞F(ω)eiωt dω\begin{aligned} f(t) &= \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} F(\omega)e^{i\omega t} \, d\omega \end{aligned}f(t)​=2π1​∫−∞∞​F(ω)eiωtdω​
(33)

To find ∣f(t)∣2|f(t)|^2∣f(t)∣2, we multiply f(t)f(t)f(t) by its complex conjugate:

∣f(t)∣2=f(t)f∗(t)=1(2π)2∫−∞∞∫−∞∞F(ω)F∗(ω′)ei(ω−ω′)t dω dω′\begin{aligned} |f(t)|^2 &= f(t)f^*(t) \\ &= \frac{1}{(2\pi)^2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} F(\omega)F^*(\omega')e^{i(\omega-\omega')t} \, d\omega \, d\omega' \end{aligned}∣f(t)∣2​=f(t)f∗(t)=(2π)21​∫−∞∞​∫−∞∞​F(ω)F∗(ω′)ei(ω−ω′)tdωdω′​
(34)

Now, we integrate both sides over all time:

∫−∞∞∣f(t)∣2 dt=1(2π)2∫−∞∞∫−∞∞F(ω)F∗(ω′)(∫−∞∞ei(ω−ω′)t dt) dω dω′\begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |f(t)|^2 \, dt &= \frac{1}{(2\pi)^2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} F(\omega)F^*(\omega')\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{i(\omega-\omega')t} \, dt\right) \, d\omega \, d\omega' \end{aligned}∫−∞∞​∣f(t)∣2dt​=(2π)21​∫−∞∞​∫−∞∞​F(ω)F∗(ω′)(∫−∞∞​ei(ω−ω′)tdt)dωdω′​
(35)

The integral in parentheses is the Dirac delta function:

∫−∞∞ei(ω−ω′)t dt=2πδ(ω−ω′)\begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{i(\omega-\omega')t} \, dt = 2\pi\delta(\omega-\omega') \end{aligned}∫−∞∞​ei(ω−ω′)tdt=2πδ(ω−ω′)​
(36)

Proof of Parseval’s Theorem - cont¶

Substituting this back into our equation:

∫−∞∞∣f(t)∣2 dt=12π∫−∞∞∫−∞∞F(ω)F∗(ω′)δ(ω−ω′) dω dω′=12π∫−∞∞F(ω)F∗(ω) dω=12π∫−∞∞∣F(ω)∣2 dω\begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |f(t)|^2 \, dt &= \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} F(\omega)F^*(\omega')\delta(\omega-\omega') \, d\omega \, d\omega' \\ &= \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} F(\omega)F^*(\omega) \, d\omega \\ &= \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |F(\omega)|^2 \, d\omega \end{aligned}∫−∞∞​∣f(t)∣2dt​=2π1​∫−∞∞​∫−∞∞​F(ω)F∗(ω′)δ(ω−ω′)dωdω′=2π1​∫−∞∞​F(ω)F∗(ω)dω=2π1​∫−∞∞​∣F(ω)∣2dω​
(37)

This completes the proof of Parseval’s Theorem.

Discrete Fourier transform (DFT)¶

The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) is a powerful tool used to transform a sequence of discrete-time signals from the time domain into the frequency domain. It is often considered an approximation or discretization of the Fourier series for signals that are sampled in time and of finite length.

Suppose f=[f0,f1,f2,…,fn−1]\mathbf{f} = [f_0, f_1, f_2, \dots, f_{n-1} ]f=[f0​,f1​,f2​,…,fn−1​] is the discretized representation of function f(x)f(x)f(x) at regular spacing Δx\Delta xΔx.

The discrete Fourier transform is given by:

f^k=∑j=0n−1fje−i2πjk/n\hat{f}_k = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} f_j e^{-i 2\pi jk /n}f^​k​=j=0∑n−1​fj​e−i2πjk/n
(38)

The inverse discrete Fourier transform is

fj=1n∑k=0n−1f^kei2πjk/n.f_j = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \hat{f}_k e^{i 2\pi jk /n}.fj​=n1​k=0∑n−1​f^​k​ei2πjk/n.
(39)

Here ωn=e−i2π/n\omega_n=e^{-i2\pi/n}ωn​=e−i2π/n is the primitive nnnth root of unity used to construct the DFT matrix. If samples are separated by Δt\Delta tΔt, frequency bin kkk corresponds to k/(nΔt)k/(n\Delta t)k/(nΔt) cycles per unit time, with negative frequencies represented by the upper-index bins.

Discrete Fourier transform (DFT) (continued)¶

Thus, DFT is a linear operator (i.e., a matrix) that maps the data points in f\mathbf{f}f to the frequency domain f^\hat{\mathbf{f}}f^:

{f0,f1,f2,…,fn−1}⇒{f^0,f^1,f^2,…,f^n−1}\{f_0, f_1, f_2, \dots, f_{n-1} \} \Rightarrow \{\hat{f}_0, \hat{f}_1, \hat{f}_2, \dots, \hat{f}_{n-1} \}{f0​,f1​,f2​,…,fn−1​}⇒{f^​0​,f^​1​,f^​2​,…,f^​n−1​}
(40)

The DFT may be computed by matrix multiplication:

[f^0f^1f^2⋮f^n−1]=[111⋯11ωnωn2⋯ωnn−11ωn2ωn4⋯ωn2(n−1)⋮⋮⋮⋱⋮1ωnn−1ωn2(n−1)⋯ωn(n−1)2][f0f1f2⋮fn−1]\begin{bmatrix} \hat{f}_0 \\ \hat{f}_1 \\ \hat{f}_2 \\ \vdots \\ \hat{f}_{n-1} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\ 1 & \omega_n & \omega_n^2 & \cdots & \omega_n^{n-1} \\ 1 & \omega_n^2 & \omega_n^4 & \cdots & \omega_n^{2(n-1)} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 1 & \omega_n^{n-1} & \omega_n^{2(n-1)} & \cdots & \omega_n^{(n-1)^2} \\ \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} f_0 \\ f_1 \\ f_2\\ \vdots \\ f_{n-1} \end{bmatrix}⎣⎡​f^​0​f^​1​f^​2​⋮f^​n−1​​⎦⎤​=⎣⎡​111⋮1​1ωn​ωn2​⋮ωnn−1​​1ωn2​ωn4​⋮ωn2(n−1)​​⋯⋯⋯⋱⋯​1ωnn−1​ωn2(n−1)​⋮ωn(n−1)2​​⎦⎤​⎣⎡​f0​f1​f2​⋮fn−1​​⎦⎤​
(41)

The displayed DFT matrix is a complex Vandermonde matrix. With this normalization it satisfies Fn†Fn=nIF_n^\dagger F_n=nIFn†​Fn​=nI and is therefore not itself unitary; Fn/nF_n/\sqrt{n}Fn​/n​ is unitary. Each output coefficient has a magnitude and phase.

Fast Fourier transform (FFT)¶

  • Discrete Fourier transform (DFT): cost O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2)

  • Fast Fourier transform (FFT): cost O(nlog⁡(n))O(n \log (n))O(nlog(n))

  • The ratio n2/(nlog⁡n)=n/log⁡nn^2/(n\log n)=n/\log nn2/(nlogn)=n/logn grows with nnn, so the computational advantage becomes dramatic for long signals.

  • Example: ten seconds sampled at 44.1 kHz gives n=441,000n=441{,}000n=441,000. The leading operation counts scale roughly as 1.94×10111.94\times10^{11}1.94×1011 for direct DFT evaluation versus 8.3×1068.3\times10^68.3×106 for nlog⁡2nn\log_2nnlog2​n FFT scaling (implementation constants vary).

  • Related factorizations date back to Gauss; Cooley and Tukey’s 1965 paper helped establish the modern FFT algorithm.

FFT algorithm¶

  • Suppose nnn is a power of 2, e.g., n=1024=210n = 1024 = 2^{10}n=1024=210.

  • Split the input into its even- and odd-indexed subsequences. For k=0,…,n/2−1k=0,\ldots,n/2-1k=0,…,n/2−1, compute the two length-n/2n/2n/2 DFTs EkE_kEk​ and OkO_kOk​. Then

f^k=Ek+ωnkOk,f^k+n/2=Ek−ωnkOk,ωn=e−i2π/n.\begin{aligned} \widehat f_k &= E_k+\omega_n^k O_k,\\ \widehat f_{k+n/2} &= E_k-\omega_n^k O_k, \qquad \omega_n=e^{-i2\pi/n}. \end{aligned}f​k​f​k+n/2​​=Ek​+ωnk​Ok​,=Ek​−ωnk​Ok​,ωn​=e−i2π/n.​
(42)

  • feven\mathbf{f}_{even}feven​ and fodd\mathbf{f}_{odd}fodd​ are the even and odd index elements of f\mathbf{f}f

  • The process is then repeated, i.e., F1024→F512→F256→⋯→F4→F2\mathbf{F}_{1024} \rightarrow \mathbf{F}_{512} \rightarrow \mathbf{F}_{256} \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow \mathbf{F}_{4} \rightarrow \mathbf{F}_{2}F1024​→F512​→F256​→⋯→F4​→F2​

  • If n≠2pn\ne2^pn=2p, one may use a mixed-radix or other general-length FFT; zero padding to a convenient length changes the frequency-grid sampling but does not add information to the signal.

FFT applications¶

What the original figure plots. It shows aperture and observation planes in a far-field diffraction geometry.

What this is trying to convey. Fourier-optics geometry from Jonathan’s original notes: the far-field pattern is related to the spatial Fourier transform of the aperture field.

Polished version.

  • Computing derivatives, e.g., to solve PDEs

  • Denoising data

  • Data analysis

  • Compression of audio and video signals

  1. Time-Shifting Property

    The time-shifting property states that a shift in the time domain corresponds to a phase shift in the frequency domain:

    If F{f(t)}=F(ω)\mathcal{F}\{f(t)\} = F(\omega)F{f(t)}=F(ω), then F{f(t−t0)}=e−iωt0F(ω)\mathcal{F}\{f(t-t_0)\} = e^{-i\omega t_0}F(\omega)F{f(t−t0​)}=e−iωt0​F(ω)

    This property is crucial in understanding how delays in signals affect their frequency content. Prove this.

Existing final-project option¶

Motivation {#motivation-3 .unnumbered}¶

The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem states that a continuous signal can be perfectly reconstructed from discrete samples if the sampling rate is at least twice the highest frequency component. Sampling below this rate causes aliasing, a phenomenon where high frequencies are misrepresented in the sampled signal.

Tasks {#tasks-4 .unnumbered}¶

  1. Generate or select a continuous-time signal with multiple frequency components.

  2. Sample the signal at different rates:

    • Above the Nyquist rate

    • At the Nyquist rate

    • Below the Nyquist rate

  3. Compute the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) of each sampled signal.

  4. Plot the reconstructed signals using sinc interpolation.

  5. Analyze and visualize the aliasing effect.

  6. Explore the use of anti-aliasing filters before sampling.

Hints {#hints-4 .unnumbered}¶

  • Use a combination of sine and cosine functions to create test signals.

  • For plotting frequency content, use FFT in Python/Matlab and compute magnitude spectrum.

  • Compare spectra at different sampling rates to identify aliasing.

  • Observe how undersampling folds high-frequency components into the lower-frequency spectrum.
